events.description: Shevardnadze, Yazov, Kryuchkov and others submit note on measures for withdrawal of Soviet forces
Politburo (Protocol 146) agrees with understandings set out in the note
Deadline for Soviet troop withdrawal under Geneva accords
Shevardnadze, Yazov and Kryuchkov submit a note on measures for the impending Soviet withdrawal.
CPSU CC Politburo agrees to the understandings in the note (Protocol No. 146).
Deadline under Geneva accords for end of the Soviet military contingent's stay in Afghanistan.
Last Soviet units to leave Kabul at the beginning of February.
Najibullah considers declaring martial law, deciding it is best done after Soviet departure.
Several thousand tons of flour delivered to Kabul by Soviet motor and air transport.
Announced date for complete withdrawal of Soviet forces from Afghanistan; the document debates whether to keep some troops after this date.
Opposition effectively carries out a blockade of the Hairaton-Kabul highway through robberies and bribery of drivers, producing flour shortages in Kabul.
Soviet motor and air transport delivers several thousand tons of flour to Kabul.
Pakistani border guards participate in military operations, bombard border regions, and arms and armed bands cross from Pakistan.
Najibullah says the regime survives if the Hairaton-Kabul road stays secure until May.
Proposed fourth scenario: leave Soviet units at key points such as Salang Pass under pretext of transferring posts, then begin convoy escort.
Proposed talks with UN Special coordinator Aga Khan on UN convoys via Pakistan and the USSR.
Soviet leadership memo with recommendations on Afghanistan: withdrawal scenarios, convoy escorts, aid, weapons transfers, propaganda, UN contacts.
Deadline for Soviet troop withdrawal from Afghanistan; scenarios leave some troops behind afterward.
Planned talks of USSR foreign minister in Islamabad with Pakistani side.
Planned talks with UN Special Coordinator Aga Khan on UN convoys via Pakistan and USSR.

sources_cited: TsKhSD, f. 89, per. 10, dok. 4 (provided by M. Kramer; trans. D. Rozas)
key_claims: Soviet leaders feared the Najibullah regime could fall soon after the 15 February 1989 withdrawal.
The Kabul regime hoped continuing splits in the opposition, notably Rabbani versus Hekmatyar, would help it survive.
The Soviets accused Pakistan of flagrant Geneva accord violations, with opposition bases and training centers in Peshawar.
Opposition economic blockade of Kabul and the Hairaton-Kabul highway, including Ahmad Shah Massoud's forces, were seen as the main threat.
Five scenarios were considered to keep some Soviet forces or convoy escorts after 15 February, including at Salang and Kabul airport.
Moscow planned to give Afghans R-300 rockets and Hurricane launchers and to split moderates from extremists via UN mediation.
